'''Yatsurugi Shrine''' (やつるぎじんじゃ) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|qid=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine}} located in {{ill|Suwa, Nagano|en|Suwa, Nagano|qid=Q846338|lt=Suwa, Nagano}}, Nagano Prefecture. Formerly classified as a {{ill|Ken-sha|ja|県社|qid=Q90139226}}{{efn|Ken-sha|WD=Q90139226|lt=Ken-sha|1=modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/village shrine|qq=ja_comment|qid=Q90139226|qq= 近代社格制度|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q712534}}, it enshrines three deities: {{ill|Ōkuninushi|en|Ōkuninushi|qid=Q276944|lt=Ōkuninushi}} as Yachihoko no Kami, {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en|Yamato Takeru|qid=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru}}, and {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|en|Emperor Ōjin|qid=Q317997|lt=Emperor Ōjin}}. It serves as a sub-shrine of the {{ill|Suwa-taisha|en|Suwa-taisha|qid=Q218813|lt=Suwa-taisha}} Upper Shrine.

== History ==
Originally located on Takashima in {{ill|Lake Suwa|en|Lake Suwa|qid=Q1206692|lt=Lake Suwa}}, the shrine was historically built using funds raised through shipbuilding taxes on Lake Suwa. During the construction of {{ill|Takashima Castle|en|Takashima Castle|qid=Q10856395|lt=Takashima Castle}} by {{ill|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|en|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|qid=Q187550|lt=Toyotomi Hideyoshi}}, the shrine was relocated to its present location. During the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|qid=Q184963|lt=Edo period}}, the {{ill|Suwa clan|en|Suwa clan|qid=Q2975376|lt=Suwa clan}}, lords of Takashima Domain, venerated the shrine as a guardian of their castle. Since the {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|qid=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era}}, it has been worshiped as the tutelary deity of Kowada Village.

== Suwa Lake Crossing Ritual ==
The shrine is notable for its unique ritual, the '''Lake-Crossing Ritual''' (みわたりしんじ). Commonly referred to as the "Observation of the Lake-Crossing Ritual," it is performed by the shrine's [[:en:Kannushi|Kannushi]] (Shinto priests). (See also {{ill|Lake Suwa|ja|諏訪湖#御神渡り|御神渡り|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Lake Suwa#Omiwatari|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q1206692}}).

When the "Omiwatari" phenomenon is observed on Lake Suwa, the shrine convenes an extraordinary council to determine the date for the observation ceremony. Prior to the ceremony, the chief priest and other shrine officials place sacred ropes ({{ill|Shimenawa|en|Shimenawa|qid=Q1887421|lt=Shimenawa}}) on their household gates and undertake a period of ritual purification ({{ill|Shōjin kessai|ja|精進潔斎|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shōjin kessai|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}). On the day of the ceremony, they perform a purification rite (修祓) at the shrine before heading to Lake Suwa.

At the lake, the priests inspect the ice formations, including the primary (一之御渡), secondary (二之御渡), and Saku no Miwatari (佐久之御渡) crossings, as well as both lower and upper shorelines. Upon returning to the shrine, a "Report Ritual" (奉告祭) is conducted to inform the enshrined deities of the lake's conditions. Based on these observations, predictions about the year’s harvest, societal fortune, and climate are made. The results are compiled into a "Report Document" (注進状) and submitted during the "Lake-Crossing Report Ceremony" (御渡注進式) at the {{ill|Suwa-taisha|lt=Suwa Taisha Upper Shrine|ja|諏訪大社#上社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Suwa-taisha|qq=}}. The shrine then forwards the information to the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|en|Imperial Household Agency|qid=Q1143602|lt=Imperial Household Agency}} and the {{ill|Japan Meteorological Agency|en|Japan_Meteorological_Agency|qid=Q860935|lt=Japan Meteorological Agency}}.<ref>During the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|qid=Q184963|lt=Edo period}}, these reports were submitted to the {{ill|Tokugawa shogunate|2=ja|3=江戸幕府|ja|Tokugawa shogunate|2=ja|3=江戸幕府|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tokugawa shogunate|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}.</ref>

The most recent instance of this ritual occurred in {{ill|2013|en|2013|qid=Q1998|lt=2013}}, with the observation on January 22, the ceremony on January 25, and the report submission on February 17. In years when the "Omiwatari" is not observed, the ritual still takes place, with a report stating "No crossing was observed." In such cases, Lake Suwa is referred to as "the opening sea" (明けの海).
